title: Next.js development

seo.title: Next.js development agency
seo.description: Next.js and React development for marketing sites, headless CMS builds, stores and portals, held to a written performance budget. From $12,000.

answerBlock: Next.js development is building websites and web applications on Next.js, the React framework for fast, server-rendered pages. Calwebtech uses it for marketing sites, headless CMS builds, B2B stores and portals that need speed and custom logic, with a content dashboard so editors keep control. Projects typically cost $12,000 to $60,000, depending on scope.

hero.outcome: Pages that load fast on a phone, content your team edits without a developer, and a codebase the next developer can read.

problem.heading: When is Next.js the right choice for a website?
problem.intro: Teams usually come to Next.js development from one of three places.

situations.title: A slow site is costing search and sales
situations.body: The current platform piles scripts and plugins onto every page, and no amount of caching gets mobile load times where they need to be.

situations.title: The site needs to do more than publish pages
situations.body: Pricing, quoting, accounts, search or integrations have outgrown what a theme and plugins can do reliably.

situations.title: Content and product live in different systems
situations.body: Marketing pages, documentation and the product each use different tools, so the brand drifts and every release breaks something.

included.heading: What is included in a Next.js build?
items: An architecture plan: which pages render on the server, which are static and what is cached
A React component library and design tokens shared across the whole site
A headless CMS or a custom content dashboard, modelled around your content types
TypeScript throughout, with validation at every boundary
Server routes or a separate Node API for forms, accounts and integrations
A written performance budget, with load time, layout shift and script weight checked in CI
Structured data, metadata, sitemaps and redirects built into the templates
WCAG 2.2 AA as the working standard
Containerised hosting on infrastructure registered in your name
Documentation, editor training and a clean handover of the repository

process.heading: How does a Next.js project run?
process.intro: Six to eight weeks for most marketing sites and headless builds, and nine to fourteen when accounts, pricing or integrations are involved.

steps.title: Discovery and architecture
steps.body: Content model, rendering strategy, integrations and the performance budget, agreed in writing with a fixed scope.

steps.title: Design system
steps.body: Tokens, components and high-fidelity screens, designed as the same components the site will be built from.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Templates, content types, forms and integrations on a staging URL, with every pull request checked against the budget.

steps.title: Prove
steps.body: Cross-browser and accessibility testing, a performance pass on real mobile conditions and a tested backup restore.

steps.title: Launch and hand over
steps.body: Cutover, redirects, monitoring, editor training and the repository handed over with its documentation.

technology.intro: A typed stack from the database to the page, so a change in one place is checked everywhere it matters.

comparison.heading: How does our Next.js development compare with the alternatives?

rows.label: Performance
rows.us: A written budget for load time, layout shift and script weight, checked in CI.
rows.pageBuilder: Builder scripts load on every page.
rows.offshore: Rarely measured unless named in the contract.

rows.label: Editing
rows.us: A headless CMS or dashboard modelled around your content types.
rows.freelancer: Often a developer-only codebase with content kept in files.
rows.pageBuilder: Easy visual editing, with little structure behind it.

rows.label: Code quality
rows.us: TypeScript, tests and reviewed pull requests from the first commit.
rows.pageBuilder: No code to review; the vendor controls it.
rows.offshore: Varies by team, and often by week.

rows.label: Hosting
rows.us: Containers on infrastructure in your name, or the host you prefer.
rows.freelancer: Often on the developer's own accounts.

rows.label: How the price is set
rows.us: A fixed price and scope, agreed before work starts.
rows.pageBuilder: Monthly fees that rise with plans and add-ons.
rows.offshore: Low day rates, with change requests adding up.

pricing.heading: How much does a Next.js website cost?
pricing.intro: Most Next.js projects land between $12,000 and $60,000. A marketing site or headless CMS build sits in the $12,000 to $25,000 band; accounts, pricing and integrations move it towards $60,000.

factors.title: Content model
factors.body: A handful of content types is quick to model. Many related types, translations or complex editorial workflows take longer.

factors.title: Headless CMS choice
factors.body: A hosted headless CMS saves build time but adds a subscription. A custom dashboard costs more up front and has no per-seat fees.

factors.title: Dynamic features
factors.body: Accounts, pricing, search and personalisation each need server logic, caching decisions and testing.

factors.title: Integrations
factors.body: CRM, ERP, booking and payment systems add build and testing time, especially older ones.

factors.title: Migration
factors.body: Moving content and URLs from WordPress or another platform needs mapping, cleaning and redirects.

faq.heading: What do buyers ask about Next.js development?

items.question: Is Next.js better than WordPress?
items.answer: Neither is better for everyone. Next.js suits sites that need speed, custom logic or integrations, and teams happy to edit in a headless CMS or dashboard. WordPress suits teams who know its editor and rely on its plugins. We recommend one in writing, with the reasons.

items.question: What is a headless CMS build?
items.answer: It separates where content is edited from how pages are built. Editors work in a CMS or dashboard and Next.js renders the pages, so the site stays fast and the same content can also feed apps, documentation or other channels.

items.question: Can our marketing team edit a Next.js site?
items.answer: Yes. Every repeatable page is a content type with its own editor in the CMS or dashboard, so publishing needs no developer and no deployment. Training and a written manual are part of the handover.

items.question: Where will a Next.js site be hosted?
items.answer: On infrastructure registered in your name. We deploy in containers behind automatic TLS, or to a managed Next.js host if your team prefers one, and the proposal sets out the running costs.

items.question: How fast will the site be?
items.answer: We agree a written performance budget for load time, layout shift and script weight before the build, and fail our own release if it is breached. The targets are set per project and measured on mobile conditions, not only on a fast desk connection.

items.question: Can you take over an existing Next.js codebase?
items.answer: Yes. We start with a code review and a written verdict on what to keep, what to fix and what to replace, with a fixed price for the work.

items.question: Who owns the code?
items.answer: You do. The repository and every account are in your name from the start, with no proprietary framework, so another developer could continue from the documentation.
